abstract: Gait variability in healthy adults exhibits Long-Range Autocorrelations (LRA), reflecting long-term statistical dependencies between stride intervals. Previous studies have interpreted LRA within an optimal control framework, where stride length and duration are regulated in a coordinated manner to maintain a constant walking speed. Such objective offers redundancy among gait parameters that achieve success. In this context, imposing constraints on the walking cadence reduces this redundancy and leads to a loss of LRA. The model therefore predicts that during free walking, stride-by-stride adjustments should be directed toward the redundant axis, whereas during cued walking, they should be directed toward the imposed target values. Consequently, differences between conditions should be observable based on a geometric characterization of changes in length and duration. With simulations and experimental data, we show that stride-by-stride adjustments discriminate between cued and free walking conditions, supporting the geometric interpretation of the model.  Moreover, this metric achieves good discrimination (Area Under the Curve = 0.74) for 50-stride series, compared with LRA estimates that typically require series of 80 strides to achieve comparable success.  In sum, our study validates a novel geometric approach to quantifying gait control strategies, supporting the emergence of LRA through flexible adjustments of stride parameters.
